text:
Your head, your gesture, your air
are lovely as a lovely landscape;
laughter plays across your face
like a fresh wind in a clear sky.

The sorrowful passerby you brush
is dazzled by the health
that springs like radiance
from your shoulders and your arms.

The riotous colors
you scatter over your clothes
make poets dream
of a lively ballet of flowers.

Your mad dresses are the emblem
of your motley spirit;
madwoman who has maddened me,
I love you as much as I hate you.

Often in the garden
through which I drag my torpor,
I have felt, like an irony,
the sun tear open my breast;

And the green and the spring
wounded my heart so deeply
that I punished upon a flower
Nature’s insolence.

So, one night, I would like,
when the hour of pleasure comes,
to creep without a sound, like a coward,
toward the treasures that adorn you,

to punish your flesh,
to bruise your unpardoned breast,
and open in your astonished side
a long and deep wound,

And—dizzying sweetness!—
through those new lips,
more dazzling and more beautiful,
to inject my venom into you, my sister.

translation.title: To One Who Is Too Gay
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The poem’s disturbing fusion of desire, envy, and violence is preserved without softening.
